analysis.one_liner: Reinstates and raises polluter taxes to refill the Superfund trust fund for cleaning up the largest toxic waste sites.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in April 2007, never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund pays to clean up the nation's worst toxic waste sites, but the special taxes on oil, chemicals, and corporations that once funded it expired in 1995, leaving taxpayers to foot the bill. This bill would have brought those taxes back permanently — and temporarily raised them by 50% — to create a dedicated account for 'megasites,' the huge, severely contaminated sites that cost $50 million or more to clean. It also would have required the EPA to report to Congress every year on cleanup progress at every Superfund site.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly one in four Americans who live within three miles of a Superfund site, communities near the largest and most dangerous contaminated sites, and state governments that otherwise inherit decades of cleanup costs. The bill's own findings note that after the polluter taxes expired, cleanup money ran short, new construction funding was blocked at numerous sites in fiscal years 2004-2006, and existing cleanups slowed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near toxic waste sites

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated Megasites and High Risk Sites Cleanup Account funded by a temporary 50% increase in the Superfund excise taxes and the corporate environmental income tax from 2008 through 2012, reserved for sites costing more than $50 million to clean or posing high health risks.

Permanently reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate and the corporate environmental income tax whenever the trust fund's unobligated balance falls below $5.7 billion, restoring a dedicated funding stream that expired in 1995.
Keeps polluters on the hook: the bill's findings state that responsible parties remain liable for hazardous releases even after the Superfund taxes are reestablished.

Requires annual EPA reports to Congress on cleanup progress, costs, cost overruns, and schedule delays at every non-Federal site on the National Priorities List, increasing public accountability for how cleanup money is spent.
The bill's findings state that one in four Americans lives within three miles of a Superfund site, and that delayed cleanups magnify public health risks and raise total cleanup costs.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that import, produce, or sell crude oil and the chemicals covered by the Superfund excise taxes — petroleum refiners and chemical manufacturers — plus corporations generally through the 0.12% environmental income tax, which the bill would temporarily raise to 0.18%. These costs can be passed to consumers in fuel and chemical prices.

drawbacks.text: The taxes are levied on the oil and chemical industries broadly rather than on the specific companies responsible for each contaminated site, so many firms that never contaminated anything would pay, and some costs would likely show up in prices for fuel and chemical products.

The temporary 50% rate increase expires after 2012, but many megasites require cleanup lasting decades or longer — the bill's own findings say more than half of mining sites on the National Priorities List will need maintenance in perpetuity — so the dedicated megasite funding is not built to match the scale or duration of the problem.
Because the taxes switch off automatically whenever the trust fund balance exceeds $5.7 billion, the funding stream is uneven by design, which could complicate long-range cleanup budgeting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, well-documented problem: after the polluter taxes lapsed in 1995, the Superfund depended on general taxpayer money, cleanups slowed, and the biggest sites were crowding out smaller ones. The main costs fall on oil and chemical companies and corporate taxpayers, with some pass-through to consumer prices, and the design is imperfect — a temporary surcharge for cleanups that may last forever. On balance it shifts a public cleanup burden back onto the industries the fund was created to make pay, which is why an honest reading favors the bill on balance.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced and never moved again — no hearing, no vote, no floor action — so it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on April 17, 2007, with a single Democratic cosponsor.

The House referred it to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure committees, which is standard for a bill touching tax and environmental law, and it went to subcommittees on Water Resources and Environment and on Environment and Hazardous Materials two days later.
No committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled in the House, and no Senate companion appears in the record; the bill expired at the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009.
Congress ultimately let the Superfund polluter taxes stay expired for the entire 110th Congress; a version of the tax was not reinstated until the 2021 infrastructure law, long after this bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil, chemical, and manufacturing companies that would have paid the reinstated Superfund taxes were better off because the bill died; the cost of cleaning up orphan toxic waste sites continued to fall on general taxpayers, and communities near the largest sites kept waiting for funds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies; cleanup costs stayed public

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on April 17, 2007.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with primary jurisdiction over the bill's tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never reported the bill out or scheduled any action on it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.role: Additional committees of referral for the environmental provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never took the bill up; their subcommittees held no recorded action after April 2007.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so party positions can only be guessed at from sponsorship: a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, with no Republicans on the bill and no record of opposition votes.

industries.note: The bill reinstates the crude oil and chemical feedstock excise taxes that expired in 1995 and raises them 50% from 2008 through 2012, directly increasing these companies' tax bills. Their gain from the bill dying is the public's cost, since expired taxes shifted Superfund cleanup funding onto general taxpayers.

The corporate environmental income tax, lapsed since 1995, would return permanently whenever the Superfund balance drops below $5.7 billion, and temporarily rise from 0.12% to 0.18%. Some of this cost passes through to consumers in prices.

industries.industry: Potentially responsible parties at Superfund sites
industries.note: The bill explicitly keeps polluters liable for hazardous releases even after the taxes return, but its dedicated megasite account also covers cleanups where no viable responsible party exists — the situation where the federal government currently pays 90% of construction costs. Companies with lingering megasite liability would face continued cleanup obligations either way.
